3473: The Six Articles on Public Security, issued in January 1967, made attacks on Mao Zedong or Lin Biao active counterrevolution. The Commune's declaration also stated that organizations like the “Honorably Discharged Veterans” would be banned at once and their ringleaders punished severely.
3474: From 1961 to 1963, Shanghai cut more than 310,000 workers, most of them older workers. Quanhongzong was a national organization founded in Beijing by temporary and contract workers. The Joint Notice it signed with the Ministry of Labor and the ACFTU had been voided by the Central Cultural Revolution Group in early January.
3475: In the Qinghai Provincial Military District, the commander Liu Xianquan backed the rebel faction August 18. His deputy Zhao Yongfu put him under house arrest and seized power in the district. Army matters belonged to the Central Military Commission.
3476: On February 12 the center ordered all nationwide mass organizations banned. Three days later Quanhongzong was declared a reactionary organization. Everywhere, the core members of reactionary organizations were then being arrested.
3477: Geng Jinzhang led the “Second Regiment” under the Workers' General Headquarters. It kept pulling in more people until headquarters could not control it. On February 11 WGHQ issued a notice exposing him. Back then, before WGHQ did anything big, it first asked whether this was what Zhang Chunqiao wanted.
3478: Fan Zuodong ran daily affairs at the Workers' General Headquarters. The first of the Standing Committee members the notice said never came to the office was Wang Hongwen. At the time a charge like “careerist, splitter” was enough to get someone locked up at a public security sub-bureau.
3479: The Shanghai Revolutionary Committee was then the highest authority in Shanghai, and Wang Hongwen acted in its name. The Support-Liansi Station said real power in it was not in proletarian hands and called for a “second great upheaval,” which meant tearing it down and starting over.
3480: Wang Hongwen led the Workers' General Headquarters and also acted in the name of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee, so both sides waited for his decision. WGHQ people found the revolutionary committee too soft. The Shanghai Revolutionary Committee wanted to command all the forces itself. The line Zhang Chunqiao set by phone in July leaned toward calm.
3481: Being labeled a “royalist” meant losing the right to take part in the movement. The two factions at Shanghai Diesel called each other that, though both were rebel organizations. The side attacking the building was directed from a command post set up beside it by people from the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee and the Workers' General Headquarters.
3482: Mao Zedong was in Shanghai these days. Whatever he nodded to was settled. He wanted to arm the left, and Shanghai's militia began forming that night. Who handed out the guns and who controlled them would decide who held armed force in Shanghai later.
3483: The Nanjing Military Region backed “August 27” and Zhang Chunqiao backed “Red General Headquarters,” so each faction had a patron. Xu Shiyou hid in the Dabie Mountains. It was Mao Zedong who told Zhang Chunqiao to invite him to Shanghai.
3484: Cleansing the Class Ranks spread nationwide after Mao Zedong endorsed it in May 1968. Every unit set up a special case group and put people with historical “problems” under isolation and investigation. At Tsinghua University alone, ten people were persecuted to death in two months.
3485: The July 3 Proclamation was issued jointly by the Central Committee, the State Council, the Central Military Commission and the Central Cultural Revolution Group. It was the highest level of order at the time. In history, the named dead in Guangxi in 1968 numbered nearly 90,000, most of them from the April 22 faction.
3486: Back then an outsider without a letter of introduction was a person of unknown origin. After the army units that supported the April 22 faction were moved out of Guangxi, its members were massacred in large numbers. Having their home units come to collect them meant handing them back to Guangxi.
3487: The Twelfth Plenum was a full session of the Central Committee. It was rare for a rebel from a factory to attend as a nonvoting delegate. When Mao Zedong introduced someone in public at the plenum, everyone there understood the weight of it.
3488: “Two participations, one reform, three-in-one combination” was the slogan of the Angang Constitution. Cadres take part in labor, workers take part in management, unreasonable rules are reformed, and workers, cadres and technicians work together. It was written on the walls of every factory. In many factories it stayed on the wall.
3489: The Ninth Party Congress was the Ninth National Congress of the Communist Party of China, held in 1969. Central Committee members were the top tier of the whole Party's leadership. Wang Hongwen was treated as a worker-peasant cadre, and his pay stayed with the No. 17 State Cotton Mill.
3490: Lin Liguo was Lin Biao's son and held a post in the air force. Wang Weiguo's Fourth Air Army also belonged to the air force. At the time, whom you ate with and whom you saw were often read as which side you were on.
3491: After September 13, Lin Biao went from successor to target of investigation, and everyone linked to his line had to be investigated. In March Wang Weiguo had attended the meeting Lin Liguo called on Yueyang Road, and he commanded troops of the Fourth Air Army.
3492: Nixon was the first American president to visit China after 1949. China and the US did not yet have diplomatic relations. On the 28th the joint communiqué was issued at the Jinjiang Hotel. In history, it came to be called the “Shanghai Communiqué.” In those years self-reliance was the line, and imports and sending people abroad were tightly restricted.
3493: The Tenth Party Congress was the Tenth National Congress of the Communist Party of China, held in August 1973. Vice Chairman was the post just below the Chairman. In history, Mao Zedong brought Wang Hongwen to Beijing in September 1972, and the Tenth Party Congress made him Vice Chairman, ranked after Zhou Enlai.
3494: By January 1971 Wang Hongwen had been elected a secretary of the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee, ranked third. When Mao Zedong personally proposed bringing a local cadre to Beijing to study, it meant the man would be given a big role. What exactly he would do, no one could say.
3495: In January 1967 Mao Zedong said that if the masses elect new cadres, let them elect. In February he said, “better to call it a revolutionary committee,” and the historical Shanghai People's Commune changed its name.
3496: “Royalist” was an insult for a conservative. Putting that label on someone said they had no right to take part in the movement. Liansi and The East Is Red at Shanghai Diesel called each other that, though both were rebel organizations.
3497: The Scarlet Guards were the workers' organization that opposed the Workers' General Headquarters back then. After Kangping Road they dissolved, and many members were left with no organization at all. To the rebels they were royalists. Anyone close to them could be seen as a royalist too.
3498: The Six Articles on Public Security were issued on January 13, 1967. Attacking Mao Zedong or Lin Biao counted as active counterrevolution. The Support-Liansi Station was started by a teaching assistant at Jiaotong University. It backed Liansi at Shanghai Diesel and aimed at the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee.
3499: In history, the Shanghai People's Commune was renamed a revolutionary committee in February 1967. The Commune's declaration had promised that the new leaders would be elected by the masses on Paris Commune principles.
3500: Royalists meant the side that defended the old Municipal Party Committee early in the movement. The Scarlet Guards were called that. Inside the Workers' General Headquarters, saying someone had a problem with their stand was a very heavy charge then.
3501: The Six Articles on Public Security made words and acts attacking Mao Zedong or Lin Biao active counterrevolution. At the time, putting up big-character posters was the main way to take a public stand. A square full of posters was public opinion.
3502: In those years technicians were often paid less than workers who joined the factory the same year, and their words carried little weight. The national pass rate for industrial products averaged only about 45 percent. “Struggle between two lines” was the heaviest verdict of the time.
3503: At the time workers and cadres were on two separate staff systems, with different pay grades and different rules on shift work. A “worker-cadre” was a worker who had been promoted but kept his worker status and his old pay.
3504: In September 1972 Wang Hongwen, a worker cadre from Shanghai, was transferred to Beijing, nominally to study. When the Chairman had someone read certain books, people then took it as a message. The Chairman never spelled out what he meant, and those below could only guess.
3505: The Tenth Party Congress was the Party's national congress. The order of the Vice Chairmen and Politburo Standing Committee members elected after it was the order of power. The Party Constitution of the Ninth Congress named Lin Biao as successor. After Lin Biao fell, that passage became a problem that had to be dealt with.
3506: In those years universities took worker-peasant-soldier students. There was no exam. Students were recommended by the masses, approved by leaders and reviewed by the school. Whether recommendation was fair depended entirely on how the unit's leaders behaved.
3507: In early 1973 Premier Zhou approved buying about 4.3 billion US dollars of complete plants from Japan and the West. It was called the 4-3 Program. Buying foreign equipment and sending people abroad to learn was, in the mouths of Jiang Qing's faction, “slavish comprador philosophy” and “crawlism.”
3508: Criticize Lin, Criticize Confucius began in early 1974, nominally aimed at Lin Biao and Confucius. Rebels who had been punished took it as a chance to turn things around. The old accounts between veteran cadres and rebels were opened again.
3509: The back door meant using parents' power and connections to get a job, a university place or into the army. Everyone knew about it then, and cadres' children used it most. Criticizing the back door mostly hit veteran cadres and people in the army.
3510: A special case group's conclusions went into the dossier. Before a person could join the Party, be promoted or be transferred, the dossier was checked first. When rebels around the country were restored to their posts in 1974, their first move was often to get back the files once used against them.
3511: Tan Qilong was Zhejiang provincial Party secretary, and by now no one listened to him. The militia was supposed to be run by the army's People's Armed Forces Departments, and guns were issued and collected on orders from the provincial Party committee and the provincial military district. A phone call from a Vice Chairman of the Central Committee would be taken below as the center's wishes.
3512: Premier Zhou was Premier of the State Council and held up the government's daily work. Once he was in the hospital, who took over became a big question. When the Chairman spoke in public of a “little faction of four,” he brought into the open what others had said in private.
3513: When the Fengqing came back from its long voyage, Jiang Qing's faction used it to attack the “slavish comprador philosophy” of the Ministry of Transport and the State Council, aiming at whoever ran the State Council. The 1970 Lushan Conference was where Lin Biao's side made its move. After Lin Biao fell, bringing up Lushan meant saying someone was plotting.
3514: Speaking out freely, airing views fully, holding great debates and writing big-character posters were together called the Four Bigs. Anyone could use them in the Cultural Revolution, and they were most often used to attack people. Once a provincial Party committee labeled a poster reactionary, its author would be dragged to a criticism meeting.
3515: The new Constitution adopted in January 1975 included the Four Bigs, but not one line protected the people who put up posters. The Guangdong Provincial Party Committee organized several hundred criticism meetings against Li Yizhe's big-character poster.
3516: Shadian was a Hui village in Yunnan. Its mosque was closed early in the Cultural Revolution, and the Hui petitioned for years to reopen it. The province called this rioting and wanted the center to step in.
3517: The Hui do not eat pork, and the mosque is where they worship. Eating pork in the mosque and throwing bones down the well broke their deepest taboo. What central leaders said when receiving delegations would be taken back by the province and the army as grounds for action.
3518: At the time, once something was labeled a counterrevolutionary armed rebellion, sending in troops was called putting down a rebellion, and the dead were counted on the rebel side. In history, such verdicts took many years to be reversed.
3519: Seventy percent achievements and thirty percent mistakes was the keynote the Chairman set. He wanted the veteran cadres and the Cultural Revolution faction to say the same thing about the Cultural Revolution. Whoever led the drafting of the resolution would have to put his name to that conclusion.
3520: Dao County and Guangxi were places of mass killing in the Cultural Revolution. In history, it was later found that of the more than 4,000 people killed in Dao County over 66 days in 1967, 90 percent were four bad elements and their children. The resolution had to pass the Politburo, and every event written into it needed both sides to agree.
3521: Being in charge of the Central Committee's daily work meant actually running the Party and the state day to day under the Chairman. In 1975 that post was Deng Xiaoping's. Replacing him meant the wind had changed.
3522: In units split into two factions during the Cultural Revolution, neither side accepted the other and each held its own ground. This was called factionalism. The 1975 rectification aimed to suppress factionalism, and on the railways those suppressed were mostly rebel leaders.
3523: The 1975 railway rectification was run as a campaign. Railway bureaus held struggle sessions against nearly 10,000 people, arrested more than 2,000 and shot more than 100. The trains did run on time. Many charges on the lists were old accounts from the first years of the Cultural Revolution.
3524: “Control, restrict and suppress” was the Cultural Revolution's phrase for attacking rules. It meant rules and regulations were used to control workers, restrict workers and suppress workers. In those years the old rules of many factories were attacked and torn down. The Angang Constitution also had a line about reforming unreasonable rules and regulations.
3525: To Jiang Qing's faction, the 1975 rectification aimed to overturn the Cultural Revolution, so they called it the Right-deviationist wind to reverse verdicts. Once the Chairman took a position, everyone who had followed the rectification was counted on the side of reversing verdicts.
3526: The Tenth Party Congress was the Party's national congress. The Vice Chairmen elected after it were the people just below the Chairman in the Party. In history, one Vice Chairman of that term really did come from Shanghai's No. 17 State Cotton Mill.
3527: Jiang Qing's faction used the Fengqing to attack the “slavish comprador philosophy” of the Ministry of Transport and the State Council. The rule for the two men being held was that they could not go back to Beijing until they had been thoroughly criticized. Whoever let them go would be standing with the Ministry of Transport.
3528: The All-China Federation of Trade Unions had been shut down, and after the Ninth Party Congress the mass organizations were gone too. The unions became ground that both the rebels and the veteran cadres wanted. At the end of 1966, temporary and contract workers had staged a sit-in at the ACFTU, demanding not to be dismissed at will.
3529: That year Deng Xiaoping was in charge of the Central Committee's daily work and ran the rectification, and its targets were exactly the rebels who had risen in the Cultural Revolution. The Shanghai militia was something Wang Hongwen had reshaped over several years. The aim was less army control and an armed force of the workers' own.
3530: Beijing crowds used the mourning for Zhou Enlai to aim at Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao and their faction. The Politburo called it organized counterrevolutionary activity, and every region had to take a stand. In Shanghai, the people running the police and the militia were all from Wang Hongwen's faction.
3531: Most of the poems going around the square cursed Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Wang Hongwen and the others. The Politburo had already called these days counterrevolutionary activity, and notebooks of copied or passed-on poems would be used as evidence.
3532: Once Mao Zedong died, who had the final say became the question. Hua Guofeng ran the center's daily work, and on big matters the provinces asked the General Office of the Central Committee for instructions as usual. Where a call went showed whom you obeyed.
3533: “Gang of Four” was what Mao Zedong said around 1974 when he criticized Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen. After his death, these four were one side in the Politburo and Hua Guofeng and Ye Jianying the other. Whether Mao Yuanxin stayed was a point of dispute between them.
3534: Wang Dongxing commanded the guard units of Zhongnanhai. For more than 20 days after Mao Zedong died, the two sides in the Politburo stayed deadlocked. Just the day before, Wang Hongwen himself had said his official's hat might be knocked off any day.
3535: Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan were also detained that night. Jiang Qing and Mao Yuanxin were taken from their residences. The Shanghai Municipal Party Committee had agreed on a code with Beijing in advance. “Myocardial infarction” meant something had happened to those few in the center.
3536: Most of the poems in the square these days cursed Jiang Qing and Zhang Chunqiao, and some cursed Wang Hongwen. The Politburo wanted to label the mourning organized counterrevolutionary activity, and its members had to vote by show of hands.
3537: The top task of 1976 was Criticize Deng. The resolution removing Deng Xiaoping from all his posts followed the Chairman's view. Not raising your hand in the Politburo meant disagreeing with the Chairman.
3538: In 1975, criticizing Jiang Qing and the others, Mao Zedong asked why they did not unite with the more than 200 Central Committee members. A Central Committee plenum is a vote of all Central Committee members, far more people than the Politburo.
3539: Deng Xiaoping was still under criticism at this time. In those days Shanghai's rebels set up liaison points and put the militia on standby. They had been preparing to take on Beijing.
3540: At Qingming some people in Shanghai also brought wreaths to People's Square. There were far fewer than in Beijing, and they were soon removed. Beijing had already labeled the mourning counterrevolutionary activity. The mill's security section dealt with exactly this kind of thing.
3541: After Beijing arrested Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan, the militia at every Shanghai factory was ordered onto combat readiness. The mill's guns and ammunition were held by the militia company. By the rules, guns and ammunition were stored apart.
3542: Ma Tianshui, Xu Jingxian and Wang Xiuzhen were the main leaders of the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee. After they were summoned to Beijing, no word came back. Shanghai had a militia with more than 200,000 firearms, and Garrison Command troops around the city.
3543: In 1975 Deng Xiaoping led the rectification, and the railways came first. From early 1976 the rectification was attacked as the “Right-deviationist wind to reverse verdicts.” Removing Deng Xiaoping from his posts was the Chairman's view.
3544: Zhang Chunqiao was the man Wang Hongwen had dealt with since Anting, the head of this Shanghai faction. The people Hua Guofeng and Ye Jianying meant to arrest that night were Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and a few others.
3545: On this path Wang Hongwen ran the unions. For these years the All-China Federation of Trade Unions had only provincial preparatory groups and had not held a congress. Anyone close to Jiang Qing and the others was now to be suspended and investigated.
3546: That night Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan were detained. Jiang Qing and Mao Yuanxin were taken from their residences. The Politburo members of worker and peasant origin, Ni Zhifu, Wu Guixian and Chen Yonggui, were not arrested that night.
3547: Shanghai was the home base of Jiang Qing and Zhang Chunqiao's faction. When the news came, the city's core members met for several nights running at Kangping Road to decide whether to use the militia. In history, the center then sent Su Zhenhua, Ni Zhifu and Peng Chong to take over in Shanghai.
